cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-4-bust-of.summary: Standing in an open sarcophagus, the psalmist raises one hand toward a small bust of the beardless Christ-Logos holding a scroll in the sky and points down with the other, recalling the psalm's last verse, 'in peace I will lie down and sleep'. To the right a priest stands at a flaming altar before a church as people bring wine and animals, the 'sacrifices of righteousness'. The figure of Christ is tiny but central to the drawing's meaning.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-4-bust-of.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-112-chris.summary: In the heavens the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, with a book and cross-staff, sits in a mandorla among angels with the sun and moon. Below, an angel helps a poor man out of the dust to take an empty seat between princes on their thrones, and the barren woman becomes a joyful mother of children. The upper drawing of folio 66r illustrates the Laudate pueri.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times in the Middle Ages: the Harley Psalter, the Eadwine Psalter and the Anglo-Catalan Psalter.

Q29385366.summary: At the heart of an openwork foliate cross, the Lamb of God strides within a roundel, while the four winged creatures of the evangelists, each holding a book, fill the spaces between the arms: the man of Matthew, the lion of Mark, the ox of Luke and the eagle of John. The plaque once adorned the cover of a luxurious Gospel book, so that the Gospels themselves were framed by Christ the sacrificial Lamb and his four witnesses.
facts: The Met notes that this plaque originally covered a deluxe binding of a now-lost Gospel book.
Its stylised symbols and interlaced foliate cross have parallels in manuscripts from the region of Benevento, including the Benedictine monastery of Monte Cassino.
The four creatures derive from John's vision in Revelation 4:6–7.

Q60745622.summary: Woven entirely in coloured wool, this large hanging shows the Virgin Mary enthroned with the Christ child on her lap, flanked by the archangels Michael and Gabriel; above them, Christ appears in a radiant glory supported by two angels. A border of medallions portrays the apostles, each named in Greek. One of the very few textile icons to survive from the early Byzantine world, it joins the incarnate child and the glorified Lord in a single, prayerful image.
facts: Egypt's dry climate preserved this fragile textile, while countless painted and woven icons elsewhere perished, including during the iconoclast controversy.
The composition borrows from Byzantine imperial art: Mary is enthroned like an empress among her court officials, here the archangels.
At nearly 1.8 metres tall and woven from more than twenty colours of wool, it was a costly object, made to hang on a wall as an icon for veneration.
The Cleveland Museum of Art acquired it in 1967; the museum notes that in its own day such a tapestry cost more than a painted icon.
